title: Block close: the shape of a life
hookLine: commandments, virtues and mercy, gathered up in love

cards: An expert in the law steps forward with a test question for Jesus. In Matthew he asks: "Master, which is the great commandment in the law?"
The law is long, and a person could spend a lifetime arguing about which part matters most. Jesus gives him two, and then says something that gathers everything up.

This block of the path has walked through Christian ethics: commandments, virtues, mercy, money, peace, the poor, the stranger, enemies, friends. Today, one last question: what holds all of that together?

teach.b: Jesus answers: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets."
Both lines come from the Torah, Deuteronomy and Leviticus. The first belongs to the Shema, the passage that opens with Hear, O Israel.
Jesus doesn't invent a new law here; he names what the law hangs on, like a coat on a hook. Paul says it his own way.
In Romans he lists commandments, do not kill, do not steal, do not covet, and says they are "briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

teach.h: LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.
teach.b: Then: "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." Fulfilling, not canceling. Love doesn't make the commandments optional.
It's what they were reaching for all along. Colossians adds a picture.

After a list of virtues, kindness, humility, patience, forgiveness, it says: "And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness." Love as the belt that holds the rest in place.

teach.h: LOVE, AND DO WHAT YOU WILL.
teach.b: Augustine, in a sermon on the first letter of John, pushed it into a short line, remembered in English as: love, and do what you will. He meant a love that sometimes says no, the way a parent does.
So here is the shape of a life, as this block has traced it: Commandments as the frame. Virtues as the habits. Mercy, peace and welcome as the practice.
And love underneath all of it.

how: Churches teach Jesus's two great commandments, love of God and love of neighbor, as a summary of Christian ethics, and teach the commandments and virtues as ways that love takes shape in daily life.

he quotes the Torah: Deuteronomy for loving God, Leviticus for loving your neighbor.
Paul says love cancels the commandments
"love is the fulfilling of the law." fulfilling, not canceling: love works no ill to a neighbor.
Colossians calls charity "the bond of perfectness"
after a list of virtues: "above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness."

games.q: an expert in the law asks you: which is the great commandment in the law? what do you answer?
o: name the single most important rule.
refuse to answer a trick question.
love God with everything, and your neighbor as yourself.
games.why: asked for one, Jesus gives two, and says all the law and the prophets hang on them.

practice: Ask what three short, plain lines could give this year its shape: call my mother on Sundays, give before I spend, say the hard thing kindly.
Let each one be a form of love, toward God if you pray, toward a neighbor, and turn them over until they're short enough to remember.

wordCard.voice: Block close. The end of this block on Christian ethics: commandments, virtues and mercy, gathered up in love, which Paul calls the fulfilling of the law.

orig.note: Greek, Romans 13:10: fulfilling, fullness. "love is the fulfilling of the law."

carryVoice: Your line: love fulfils it all. Tomorrow a new block begins: the great thinkers. That closes this block.
